stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: At a flooded quarry on India's Deccan Plateau, archaeologist Nadia Okafor and her team recovered more than four hundred stone chisels dating to roughly the third century BCE. The tools were remarkably uniform ______ the same notched tip, a detail suggesting that a single workshop may have supplied the entire quarry.
choices: uniform, nearly all of them bore
uniform; nearly all of them bearing
uniform; nearly all of them bore
uniform nearly all of them bore
explanation: You need two checks here. "The tools were remarkably uniform" is a complete sentence, and so is "nearly all of them bore the same notched tip." A semicolon can join two complete sentences. It only works because "bore" is a conjugated verb, which makes the second part able to stand alone.

A.why: You joined two complete sentences with only a comma. That is a comma splice, even though the two ideas are closely related.

B.why: You saw the semicolon and stopped checking. "Bearing" is not a main verb, so "nearly all of them bearing the same notched tip" is a fragment, and a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

D.why: You ran two complete sentences together with no punctuation, which makes a fused sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Many stars that look solitary in early photographic surveys turn out, on closer inspection, to have partners. Reexamining glass plates stored for decades at an observatory in Chile, astronomer Tomás Reyes identified something the original observers ______ faint companion star circling the red giant once every 41 years.
explanation: What comes before the blank, "astronomer Tomás Reyes identified something the original observers had overlooked," is a complete sentence. That means a colon can follow it. What comes after is a phrase naming the "something," and a colon can introduce anything, including a phrase.

A.why: You used a semicolon before "a faint companion star...," which is a fragment with no main verb. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

C.why: You put the colon inside the verb phrase "had overlooked." The text before it isn't a complete sentence, and the colon splits the verb in two.

D.why: You ended the sentence with a period, which leaves "A faint companion star circling the red giant once every 41 years" on its own as a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Musicologist Ines Varga has spent a decade studying lute music from sixteenth-century Italy. Her current focus is a book of tablature that has puzzled scholars for generations. The book, which survives only in a single manuscript that a scribe copied in Padua around 1540 ______ fingerings that appear in no other known source.
explanation: The comma after "The book" opens an interruption: "which survives only in a single manuscript that a scribe copied in Padua around 1540." The interruption has to close with a matching comma. Cross it out and you get "The book preserves fingerings...," which is a correct sentence.

A.why: You closed an interruption that opened with a comma by using a dash. The punctuation around an interruption has to match at both ends.

B.why: You lost track of the long interruption and left out the closing comma. The phrase that began after "The book," is never closed off.

C.why: You put a semicolon between the subject "The book" and its verb "preserves." Neither side can stand alone as a sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Hairline cracks in plastic components often spread unseen until a part fails outright. To address this problem, chemists have begun designing materials that repair themselves. The self-healing polymer developed by a team at the University of Leeds ______ microscopic capsules of liquid resin that burst open and harden whenever a crack reaches them.
explanation: "The self-healing polymer developed by a team at the University of Leeds" is one long subject, and "contains" is its verb. "Microscopic capsules" is the object of that verb. Nothing should separate a subject from its verb or a verb from its object, so no punctuation is correct.

B.why: You felt a long subject needed a pause and added a single comma between the subject and its verb. No comma opened an interruption earlier, so there is nothing for this one to close.

C.why: You put a semicolon between the subject and its verb. Neither "The self-healing polymer developed by a team at the University of Leeds" nor "contains microscopic capsules..." is a complete sentence.

D.why: You put a colon between "contains" and its object. The text before the colon isn't a complete thought, because "contains" still needs something to contain.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Cold-water immersion is widely used by athletes hoping to recover quickly between competitions. In a study of 36 collegiate sprinters, participants who spent ten minutes in 12°C water reported less muscle soreness than those who rested normally ______ performance in the following day's 100-meter trials was no better than that of the control group.
explanation: The text on each side of the blank is a complete sentence. "However" is not a FANBOYS conjunction, so it can't join them with just a comma. A semicolon goes between the two sentences, and "however," followed by a comma, opens the second one, where the contrast belongs.

A.why: You treated "however" like "but." With only commas around it, the two complete sentences form a comma splice.

B.why: You put no punctuation between the two complete sentences, so they run together into a fused sentence.

C.why: You put the semicolon after "however," which attaches the contrast word to the first sentence. The contrast is with what follows, so "however" has to start the second sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To test whether a new drought-tolerant sorghum variety performs consistently across climates, agronomists planted it at three sites with similar rainfall but very different soils: one near Lleida, Spain ______ outside Fresno, California; and one near Bendigo, Australia. Yields varied by less than 8 percent among the sites.
explanation: The list items already contain commas ("Lleida, Spain"), so semicolons have to separate the items themselves. The text already uses a semicolon after "California," and the first item needs the same mark to stay parallel.

B.why: You used a comma to separate list items that already contain commas. That makes it impossible to tell where one site ends and the next begins, and it breaks the semicolon pattern the text sets after "California."

C.why: You used a second colon inside a list that a colon has already introduced. A colon introduces a list; it doesn't separate the items in one.

D.why: You left out punctuation between two list items, which runs "Spain" and "one outside Fresno" together.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When linguist Aiyana Begay began her fieldwork in 2009, fewer than fifty fluent speakers of the language remained. Over the next twelve years, she recorded more than two hundred hours of everyday conversation among them ______ collection that now forms the largest audio archive of any language in the region.
explanation: What comes before the blank is a complete sentence. What comes after, "a collection that now forms the largest audio archive...," is a fragment that renames the recordings. With a sentence followed by a fragment, a comma is the right choice.

A.why: You used a semicolon before a fragment. "A collection that now forms the largest audio archive..." has no main verb of its own, and a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

B.why: You ended the sentence with a period, which leaves "A collection that now forms..." standing alone as a fragment.

D.why: You left out punctuation, so "among them a collection" reads as though the collection were one of the speakers. The descriptive phrase needs a comma to set it off.
